notes.h: Tenant grievances and the limits of the 1870 Land Act
notes.b: Most Irish farmers were tenants at will or on short leases, and the law gave them little protection against eviction or rent increases. Gladstone's first big Irish reform tried to help them, but it left the central problem untouched, and that failure is why a mass land movement followed.
points: Land was owned by a small landlord class, mostly Protestant and often absentee (living elsewhere); most farmers rented their holdings, usually without a lease, and paid rent to the landlord or his agent.
Memory of the Great Famine (1845-50) and of the evictions that followed it made insecurity feel especially threatening, because a tenant who lost his holding had nowhere else to live.

The tenants' grievances were insecurity, rack-renting (very high rents), eviction and no payment for improvements they had made. Their three demands became known as the Three Fs: fair rent, fixity of tenure (the right to stay while paying rent) and free sale of the tenant's interest in the holding.

Ulster had the Ulster Custom, a tradition of tenant right that let an outgoing tenant sell his interest in his holding. Gladstone's Land Act of 1870 gave it legal force, though protection for tenants elsewhere was weak.
The Landlord and Tenant (Ireland) Act of 1870 offered compensation for improvements and for disturbance (eviction other than for non-payment of rent), but it did not control rents.

Landlords could therefore still raise rents beyond what tenants could pay and then evict for non-payment, which the Act did not forbid. This left tenants without real security of tenure, the main reason for the later land agitation.
The purchase clauses (the Bright clauses) offered loans to help tenants buy their holdings, but they were little used, so little land changed hands under them.
There is more on earlier land legislation in the notes on Ireland before 1870.
notes.tip: Keep the Acts apart: the 1870 Act did not fix rents, whereas the 1881 Act brought in the Three Fs and land courts. Examiners expect you to say what each Act did and one limit.

notes.h: The agricultural depression and the founding of the Land League (1877-1879)
notes.b: A farming crisis turned long-standing grievances into a mass movement. Michael Davitt supplied the organisation, and Charles Stewart Parnell the national leadership.
points: From 1877 poor harvests, falling prices and cheap American grain imports hit Irish farmers hard, and the wet summer of 1879 brought a partial potato failure, which reminded people of the Famine.
Rent arrears (unpaid rent) mounted, so evictions rose sharply: about 460 families were evicted in 1877 and more than 2,000 in 1880.

The New Departure of 1878 linked Fenians (revolutionaries in the IRB), land agitation and constitutional politics. Davitt met John Devoy of Clan na Gael, the Irish-American Fenian organisation, in the USA. There is more on this in the notes on the Home Rule movement.
Davitt organised a meeting at Irishtown, Co. Mayo, on 20 April 1879 against a landlord's high rents, which showed that tenants could be drawn into open protest.
At Westport in June 1879 Parnell told tenants to keep a firm grip of their homesteads (the farms and houses they lived in). This was his first major public identification with the agitation.
The Land League of Mayo was founded in August 1879. The Irish National Land League followed in Dublin in October 1879, with Parnell as president and Davitt as a leading organiser.

The League's programme was to reduce rents first and then to make tenants owners of their land, known as peasant proprietorship. Davitt personally favoured land nationalisation (state ownership of the land).
Funds came from Irish America: Parnell and John Dillon toured the United States in 1880 raising money, and Land League branches multiplied across the south and west in 1880.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Land League of Mayo (August 1879) with the Irish National Land League (October 1879, Dublin). For political agitation, credit Davitt with organising and Irishtown, and Parnell with national leadership.

notes.h: The Land War: boycotting, the Ladies' Land League and coercion (1880-1881)
notes.b: The League fought evictions with collective action rather than force, and the government answered with coercion (emergency laws that restrict normal rights). This struggle is known as the Land War.
points: The League's methods included rent strikes, in which tenants refused to pay unless rents were cut, and the shunning of anyone who profited from an eviction.
At Ennis in September 1880 Parnell urged that anyone who took a farm from which a tenant had been evicted should be shunned by the whole community, which is the policy that gave us the word boycott.
The first victim was Captain Charles Boycott, agent for Lord Erne at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, whose workers and tradesmen left him in 1880. The word boycott entered the language.

In November 1880 about fifty Orange labourers from the north were brought in to save Boycott's harvest, guarded by about 1,000 soldiers and police. The huge protection for so few workers made the operation a national joke.
Moonlighting, the night-time maiming of cattle and attacks on property, accompanied the campaign. Parnell's opponents, unionists and many Liberals, blamed the League for this agrarian crime.

The Ladies' Land League, a separate organisation led in Dublin by Anna Parnell (Parnell's sister) from early 1881, kept the campaign going when the men were jailed and helped evicted families with huts and relief. It was dissolved in 1882.
Gladstone's Chief Secretary, W.E. Forster, secured the Protection of Person and Property Act in March 1881, allowing detention without trial, so hundreds of local leaders were jailed.
Parnell's obstruction of the coercion bill in the Commons in early 1881 contributed to the introduction of closure (a rule allowing a debate to be ended by vote).
notes.tip: Know the Land League and the Ladies' Land League as two bodies, and know that Boycott is a person, not Balfour. Davitt's re-arrest in February 1881 belongs with coercion.

notes.h: The 1881 Land Act and its limits
notes.b: The 1881 Act met most of the League's demands on paper. It gave tenants what the 1870 Act had withheld, though some tenants were left out at first.
points: The Land Law (Ireland) Act (August 1881) granted the Three Fs: fair rents set by land courts, fixity of tenure while the tenant paid the rent, and free sale of the tenant's interest. A body called the Land Commission oversaw the system.
The courts fixed fair (judicial) rents for fifteen years, and the first judicial rents cut rents by about one fifth on average, a real gain for tenants.
The landlord kept ownership but shared control of the holding with the tenant, a system known as dual ownership. This is why the Act did not end landlordism, only weakened it.
Leaseholders and tenants in arrears were excluded at first, so some of the poorest tenants did not benefit until the Arrears Act of 1882 dealt with arrears.
notes.tip: Say what the 1881 Act did (the Three Fs, land courts, fifteen-year judicial rents, dual ownership) and one limit. It is the key date in any answer comparing agitation with legislation.

notes.h: Test cases, the No Rent Manifesto and the Kilmainham settlement (1881-1882)
notes.b: Parnell did not want the League to accept the Act without testing it, which led to a clash with Gladstone. The crisis ended with the League suppressed and a deal that helped tenants in arrears.
points: Parnell advised testing the Act by sending selected test cases to the land courts, in effect telling tenants to wait rather than rush in.
Gladstone denounced Parnell at Leeds on 7 October 1881, and Parnell was arrested on 13 October 1881 and held in Kilmainham.
The League replied with the No Rent Manifesto on 18 October 1881, telling tenants to pay no rent. The manifesto failed to win broad support, and the Catholic hierarchy opposed it.
The Land League was suppressed on 20 October 1881, two days after the manifesto, which ended it as an open organisation.

The Kilmainham settlement of spring 1882 was an understanding between Parnell and the government, and Parnell was released in May 1882. Do not confuse it with his imprisonment in Kilmainham in 1881-82.
The Arrears Act (August 1882) cleared arrears of rent for tenants with small valuations (rent under £30), with the state contributing. It helped those left out in 1881.
The Irish National League replaced the suppressed Land League in October 1882.
notes.tip: Get the October 1881 sequence in order: Leeds speech on 7 October, Parnell's arrest on 13 October, the manifesto on 18 October, suppression on 20 October. Do not mix the Arrears Act of 1882 with the Ashbourne Act of 1885.

notes.b: When prices fell again in 1885-86, a new campaign sought rent reductions estate by estate rather than nationally. It was a local, organised version of the earlier rent campaign.
points: The Plan of Campaign was launched in October 1886 in United Ireland by William O'Brien, John Dillon and Timothy Harrington, not by Parnell or Davitt.
Tenants on an estate offered a reduced rent. If the landlord refused, they paid it into a fund held by trustees, which supported evicted tenants.
It was applied on estates such as those of Lord Clanricarde in Co. Galway, the Vandeleur estate at Kilrush, Co. Clare, and Lord Massereene in Co. Louth.
Arthur Balfour, Chief Secretary from 1887, answered with the Criminal Law and Procedure (Ireland) Act of 1887, called the Crimes Act, allowing trial by magistrates without a jury for listed offences.
On 9 September 1887 police fired on a crowd at Mitchelstown, Co. Cork, killing three. Nationalists called it a massacre, and Balfour was nicknamed Bloody Balfour.
A papal rescript from the Holy Office in Rome condemned the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in April 1888, an unwelcome intervention for nationalists because most of them were Catholics.
Parnell was never close to the Plan because the Liberal alliance mattered more to him. The movement was weakened by the Parnell split of 1890-91.
notes.tip: Distinguish the Plan of Campaign (1886, estate by estate, led by O'Brien, Dillon and Harrington) from the Land League (1879, national). For the Crimes Act and Mitchelstown, name Arthur Balfour, not his brother Gerald.

notes.h: Constructive unionism: land purchase and the Congested Districts Board
notes.b: Conservative governments tried to defuse the land question by funding tenants' purchase of their farms. The policy is called constructive unionism, or killing Home Rule with kindness, because it hoped reform would reduce support for nationalism.
points: The Ashbourne Act (1885), passed by Salisbury's Conservative government (Lord Ashbourne), advanced loans of the full purchase price to tenants who bought from willing landlords, repayable by annuities (fixed yearly payments).
Arthur Balfour's Land Purchase Act (1891) extended the funds for purchase, so that more tenants could buy.
The Congested Districts Board (1891) targeted the poor, overcrowded districts of the west. It bought and divided estates and aided fisheries, crafts and farming.
Gerald Balfour's Land Act (1896), by Arthur's brother, made minor changes to the purchase terms, and little changed in practice.
Defenders of constructive unionism say it removed a major grievance by turning tenants into owners.
Critics argue that it made landlords richer, because they sold on good terms, while the problem of poor western farms remained.
notes.tip: Learn each Act with its date and minister (Ashbourne 1885, Arthur Balfour 1891, Gerald Balfour 1896). Strong answers also weigh critics against defenders of the policy.

notes.h: The Land Conference, the Wyndham Act and the Birrell Act (1902-1914)
notes.b: A negotiated settlement between landlords and tenant leaders brought mass tenant purchase. This was the peaceful end of the long conflict, and the state paid for it.
points: The Land Conference met in Dublin in December 1902, with landlord and tenant representatives: Lord Dunraven (chair), Captain John Shawe-Taylor, William O'Brien and John Redmond, among others. It proposed a purchase scheme with a bonus to landlords.
The Wyndham Act (1903), introduced by the Chief Secretary George Wyndham, offered tenants loans of the full price repayable over about 68 years at low interest.
Landlords received a bonus of 12 per cent of the price as an inducement to sell.
More than 200,000 tenants bought or agreed to buy within about six years. The bonus proved costly to the Treasury, so the terms were revised.

The Labourers (Ireland) Act (1906), a Liberal measure, provided for cottages for farm labourers, with tens of thousands built by 1914. The Evicted Tenants Act (1907) enabled reinstatement of tenants evicted in the Land War.
The Birrell Land Act (1909), named for the Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, allowed compulsory purchase where landlords refused to sell and gave stronger powers to the Estates Commissioners.
By 1914 most tenants had bought, or were buying, their holdings, and landlordism was finished as a political and social force. Tenant proprietorship (tenants owning their farms) had replaced it.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Wyndham (1903) with Birrell (1909). Ordinary Level questions ask who passed which Act and what it did, such as purchase loans in 1903, plus one limit.

notes.b: Davitt was the son of an evicted Mayo tenant who became a Fenian, then the organiser of the Land League and later a voice for labour. He was both a leader of the land movement and its historian.
points: Born in 1846 at Straide, Co. Mayo, he was evicted with his family in 1850 and grew up in Haslingden, Lancashire. He lost his right arm in a cotton-mill accident aged 11, and educated himself while working.

He joined the IRB (the Fenian movement), was arrested for arms trafficking in 1870 and sentenced to fifteen years. He was held at Dartmoor and released on licence in December 1877, after about seven years.

Through the New Departure he linked Fenians with the land movement, organised the Irishtown meeting in April 1879 and founded the Land League of Mayo in 1879. He was the main organiser beside Parnell's national leadership.
He was re-arrested in February 1881 and held at Portland until May 1882. His prison experience produced Leaves from a Prison Diary (1885).
He argued for land nationalisation and was dismayed that the League accepted peasant proprietorship. He opposed violence against individuals, and his social radicalism set him apart from Parnell.
In 1890 he opposed Parnell's continued leadership after the O'Shea divorce, and he founded the newspaper Labour World in the same year.

He resigned his seat in 1899 in protest at the Boer War, published The Fall of Feudalism in Ireland in 1904, and died in 1906. As both participant and writer, he left the best insider account of the movement.
Contemporaries saw him as a dangerous agitator (unionists) or a hero of the tenants (nationalists). Historians now stress his social radicalism and how he joined Fenians and constitutionalists.
notes.tip: For Davitt, give dated facts: birth at Straide, eviction in 1850, the IRB and fifteen-year sentence, release in 1877, Irishtown, the Land League, then nationalisation or labour work. For Davitt against Parnell, give each man's specific contribution and a judgement.

notes.h: Assessment: land agitation and land reform
notes.b: The land campaign changed who owned Irish land, but it was less successful in solving rural poverty and in delivering Home Rule. Judgement questions reward paired points: what was won and what was left undone.
points: Achievement: agitation forced the state to concede the Three Fs in 1881 and then to finance the transfer of land from landlords to tenants by 1914.
Limit: the settlement came through state funding and compromise, not land nationalisation, so labourers and small western farmers gained least.
Achievement: the Land League mobilised a mass base, which made Parnell's party a national force.
Limit: the agitation depended on Parnell's control, and violence, divisions over the Plan of Campaign and the papal condemnation weakened it.
Contemporary unionists claimed concessions were extracted by intimidation, while nationalists said that only pressure had moved Westminster.
Historians differ on whether constructive unionism worked: it removed a major grievance, but did not stop the growth of nationalism.
Davitt's social vision (land nationalisation, labour rights) was more radical than Parnell's, who favoured peasant proprietorship.
notes.tip: State a clear judgement early, such as that reform was largely achieved, then support it with dated points from each phase. Separate agitation (the cause of change) from legislation (the response).

keyTerms.definition: Organised public pressure for change, such as meetings, boycotts, rent campaigns and parliamentary tactics, used here to press the land question.
The tenants’ demands for fair rent, fixity of tenure and free sale of the tenant’s interest.
The period of mass agitation from 1879 to 1882, marked by rent strikes, boycotting, evictions and agrarian crime.
The social and economic isolation of a person who offended the tenants’ cause, named after Captain Charles Boycott in 1880.
Night-time agrarian violence such as cattle maiming and attacks on property carried out in the Land War.
The arrangement under the 1881 Act in which landlord and tenant both had legal interests in the same holding.
The 1886 strategy by which tenants on an estate offered a reduced rent collectively and paid it into a fund if the landlord refused.
The Conservative policy of combining coercion with land purchase and economic reform to weaken support for Home Rule.
The system, reached by 1914, in which tenants became owner-occupiers by buying their land with state loans.
The body set up in 1891 to relieve poverty in overcrowded western districts by improving land, fisheries and industries.
